1:
Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) begins by discounting the opening formula: the same phrase stands at the head of the previous chapter and has no chronological significance, so it fixes nothing about when these events fell. What it introduces, he explains, is a fuller treatment of matter already glanced at — the conflict with Ammon, touched on earlier, is now to be described at length, and in connection with it the overthrow of Hadadezer is related a second time with additional details. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) sets out the same ground as an argument of the chapter, running from the congratulatory message to Hanun and the incivility shown the messengers, through the hiring of two and thirty thousand chariots and the siege, to Joab’s defeat of the Syrians and Ammonites, the killing of Shophach their general, and the Syrians’ abandoning of the Ammonites to make peace.

Ellicott then collates the two accounts clause by clause, and his verdict varies. The name of Nahash, he notes, Samuel omits while adding Hanun, and he judges the omissions in each to be perhaps accidental; the title sons of Ammon he takes to call attention to their tribal organisation. The remainder of that verse he thinks made more perspicuous here than in Samuel by slight changes and additions. But at the next verse he will not give the chronicler the credit: the question put into the Ammonite princes’ mouths, whether David’s servants have not come to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land, is hardly an improvement on Samuel, who has them speak of searching the city, meaning the capital, and spying it out and overthrowing it. On that difference he reports the versions divided, the Syriac and the Arabic agreeing with Samuel in reading city while the Greek and the Latin read land.

On the outrage done to the messengers the two voices pull in opposite directions. Ellicott observes that Samuel specifies the shaving of half their beards, and that where the garments were cut the chronicler has substituted a more decorous term than the one appearing in Samuel, rendering it literally as unto the extremities; the cutting itself, he adds, was to make them look like captives. Clarke restores precisely what the chronicler softened, giving the plain sense in Latin and citing the Targum and Jarchi and others for it, that the men were exposed in what nature and decency require to be concealed.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) leaves the collation alone and reads the opening for its duties. It becomes good people to be neighbourly and especially to be grateful: David will pay respect to Hanun because he is his neighbour, and religion teaches us to be civil and obliging to all, to honour all men and to be ready to do all offices of kindness to those we live among, nor must difference in religion be any obstruction to it. Beyond neighbourliness there was a debt, since David remembered the kindness Hanun’s father had shown him; and those who have received kindness must return it as they have ability and opportunity, returning it to the children when those who showed it are gone. For what followed Henry reaches for the proverb of the ancients, that wickedness proceeds from the wicked.
6:
At this point Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) argues that the chronicler leaves his predecessor behind. Up to here, he says, the narrative has substantially coincided with the account in Samuel and might have been derived immediately from it; but this verse and those following differ considerably from the older account and add one or two material facts, which suggest another source altogether. He finds a mark of lateness in the wording too, the verb for making themselves odious appearing in a unique Aramaized form of the same verb Samuel uses, and glosses the phrase as having become in bad odour. On the price paid he notes that the talent was a weight and not a coin, coined money being unknown at that epoch, and reckons the thousand talents of silver at some four hundred thousand pounds.

Whether the muster agrees with Samuel’s is disputed. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) totals the older account and finds a mismatch: twenty thousand Syrians of Beth-rehob and Zoba, a thousand of Maacah and twelve thousand of Ish-tob, thirty-three thousand in all, with no mention there of chariots or cavalry; and he concludes that these cannot have been the whole army. Ellicott holds the two in substantial accord, allowing that the account the chronicler followed did not state the relative strength of the contingents but observing that the totals answer each other, thirty-two thousand with the Maachathite contingent here against thirty-two thousand with a thousand Maachathites there; the expression thirty-two thousand chariotry, he adds, is not to be pressed, the writer wishing to stress chariots and cavalry as the chief arm of the Aramaean states while being as concise as possible. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) glosses the word the same way, of thirty-two thousand men who fought partly from chariots and partly on foot with them or attending upon them, as the ancient manner of fighting was. Clarke meets a second difference by chronology rather than arithmetic: the chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia are not mentioned in the parallel place, and probably did not arrive until the Ammonites and their other allies had already been defeated in the first battle.

The battle itself is described as a problem of two fronts. Ellicott renders the clause literally, that the front of the battle had become towards Joab, front and rear, and notes that the order of words differs in Samuel with a preposition added; the Ammonites lay in front of the city while their Aramaean allies stood at some distance in the plain, so that for Joab to attack either with his whole army would have left him exposed to the other. He identifies the city as Medeba, and notes that Samuel repeats the names of the allied kings where this account does not.

Joab’s words to his brother are read for their Hebrew. Ellicott points out that the same verb underlies both halves of the exhortation, the second in reflexive form, so that the whole runs literally be strong, and let us shew ourselves strong; and that the committal to God runs, in the Hebrew order, and Jehovah — the good in his own eyes may he do. He notes also that the word for succour here is a less frequent synonym of the usual term, and that where this account has I will help thee Samuel has I will march to succour thee. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the lesson from the Ammonites instead, that the hearts of sinners marked for ruin are hardened to their destruction: seeing they had made themselves odious to David it would have been their wisdom to desire conditions of peace and offer satisfaction for the injury, the rather because they had made themselves obnoxious to the justice of God, who is King of nations and will assert the injured rights and maintain the violated laws of nations; instead of which they prepared for war.
16:
Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) uses the second muster to fix which campaign this is. Where Samuel has Hadarezer send and draw forth his forces, this account has the Syrians send messengers; and the form of the name, he says, is important as helping to identify this campaign with the one described earlier in the book. Of the river beyond which the reinforcements came he gives the Euphrates its names in turn, as the Babylonians and Assyrians called it, as the Arabs call it, and as the ancient Persians did, deriving the whole from an Accadian compound meaning great river.

One place-name he thinks the chronicler has quietly removed. Samuel says the armies came to Helam; this account says only that David came upon them, and Ellicott judges that an intelligible phrase has been substituted for the name of an unknown locality. He notes that the Hebrew for to Helam carries the same consonants as the prepositional phrase standing here, with one letter over, so that the substitution was easily made; and he reports a suggestion made to him privately by Professor Sayce, that this mysterious Helam is no other than Aleppo, the Halman of the Assyrian monuments.

The casualty figures differ, and he declines to adjudicate. This account gives seven thousand chariotry and forty thousand footmen where Samuel reads seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen; such deviations, Ellicott says, seem to indicate independent sources, and we can hardly choose between the two accounts, though he allows that horsemen may be the more correct of the two readings. The killing of Shophach he takes to be an abridged statement of what Samuel gives more fully.

The closing verse yields the sharpest observation of the chapter, from a single word. Where this account has the tributaries make peace with David and become his servants, Samuel has them make peace with Israel and serve them. To the writer of Samuel, Ellicott concludes, God’s people is the main topic, while to the chronicler it is the divinely anointed king, so that the difference, slight as it is, is characteristic of each. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) turns the submission into counsel: let those who have in vain stood it out against God be thus wise for themselves and become his servants, for they are undone if they remain his enemies.
